questions.questionText: What are the three accountabilities (roles) in Scrum?

options.text: Project Manager, Developer, and Tester
Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers
Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Development Team
Business Analyst, Scrum Master, and Engineering Team

explanation.correct: Per the 2020 Scrum Guide, the three accountabilities are: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers (no longer called 'Development Team' â€” the team as a whole is the Scrum Team).
explanation.incorrect: The 2020 Scrum Guide changed 'Development Team' to 'Developers'. The Scrum Team consists of Product Owner + Scrum Master + Developers.
explanation.examTip: 2020 Scrum Guide update: 'Development Team' â†’ 'Developers'. The whole group (PO + SM + Devs) = 'Scrum Team'. Know this for PSM I.

questions.questionText: What is the PRIMARY accountability of the Product Owner in Scrum?

options.text: Managing the Scrum Team and removing impediments
Maximising the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
Writing user stories and acceptance criteria for each sprint
Ensuring all Developers have the technical skills needed

explanation.correct: The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product and the work of the Scrum Team. They do this by managing the Product Backlog effectively.
explanation.incorrect: Managing the team and removing impediments = Scrum Master. Writing user stories is one practice but not the PO's primary accountability. Technical skills = Developers' responsibility.
explanation.examTip: PO = value maximisation through effective Product Backlog management. PO decides WHAT the team builds and in what order.

questions.questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the Scrum Master's role?

options.text: The Scrum Master manages the Scrum Team and assigns tasks to Developers
The Scrum Master is a servant leader who helps the Scrum Team and organisation understand and enact Scrum
The Scrum Master is responsible for the quality of the product delivered
The Scrum Master represents the stakeholders and prioritises the Product Backlog

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master is a servant leader â€” they serve the Scrum Team, the Product Owner, and the organisation by helping everyone understand and enact Scrum, coaching, facilitating, and removing impediments.
explanation.incorrect: The SM doesn't manage or assign tasks (self-managing team). Quality = Developers' responsibility. PO manages the backlog and represents stakeholders.
explanation.examTip: SM serves three entities: the Developers (coaching, removing impediments), the PO (backlog management help), and the Organisation (Scrum adoption).

questions.questionText: What are the three Scrum artifacts?

options.text: Sprint plan, burndown chart, and release plan
Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment
User stories, acceptance criteria, and test results
Product roadmap, sprint backlog, and velocity chart

explanation.correct: The three Scrum artifacts are: Product Backlog (ordered list of all work), Sprint Backlog (sprint plan + selected items + improvement actions), and Increment (sum of all Done work).
explanation.incorrect: Burndown charts, roadmaps, and velocity charts are tools but not Scrum artifacts. User stories and acceptance criteria are techniques, not artifacts.
explanation.examTip: Each artifact has a commitment: Product Backlog â†’ Product Goal, Sprint Backlog â†’ Sprint Goal, Increment â†’ Definition of Done.

questions.questionText: Who owns the Product Backlog in Scrum?

options.text: The Scrum Master
The Developers
The Product Owner
The stakeholders

explanation.correct: The Product Owner is solely accountable for the Product Backlog â€” its content, availability, and ordering. Others may add items but the PO decides priority and what stays.
explanation.incorrect: The Scrum Master facilitates but doesn't own the backlog. Developers can contribute but don't own it. Stakeholders can express needs but the PO manages the backlog.
explanation.examTip: PO owns Product Backlog. Developers own Sprint Backlog. The whole Scrum Team owns the Definition of Done.

questions.questionText: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Scrum?

options.text: The acceptance criteria written by the Product Owner for each Product Backlog item
A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required to be considered complete
The list of tasks that the Developers must complete in each sprint
The criteria used to determine when a sprint is ready to begin

explanation.correct: The Definition of Done is a shared understanding of what 'complete' means for any Increment â€” it ensures transparency and quality. Every Increment must meet the DoD before being considered releasable.
explanation.incorrect: Acceptance criteria are story-specific. Tasks are the developer's plan. Sprint readiness is related to Definition of Ready.
explanation.examTip: DoD = Increment quality standard. If an item doesn't meet DoD, it cannot be included in the Increment or presented at Sprint Review. It goes back to the Product Backlog.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team is working on a product. The organisation has a Definition of Done that requires all items to pass security testing. During sprint review, it is discovered that a completed item has not passed security testing.
questions.questionText: What should happen to this item?

options.text: Accept it into the Increment but create a follow-up task for security testing next sprint
It cannot be included in the Increment â€” it should be returned to the Product Backlog for future consideration
The Scrum Master should approve an exception for this sprint only
The Product Owner can accept it if the business value is high enough

explanation.correct: If an item doesn't meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be declared Done or included in the Increment. It is returned to the Product Backlog â€” the work already done is not lost but the item is not 'Done'.
explanation.incorrect: No exceptions to the DoD are allowed. The Scrum Master cannot override it. The PO cannot override it based on value. The DoD is non-negotiable.
explanation.examTip: DoD is non-negotiable. If not Done, it's not Done â€” no exceptions regardless of business value, deadline, or authority. Return to Product Backlog.

questions.questionText: What is the recommended size for a Scrum Team?

options.text: Exactly 7 people
10 or fewer people
Between 5 and 9 people not including the Scrum Master and Product Owner
As many people as needed to complete the work

explanation.correct: The 2020 Scrum Guide recommends 10 or fewer people for the entire Scrum Team (including the Scrum Master and Product Owner). Small teams are more nimble and communicate better.
explanation.incorrect: Earlier Scrum Guides suggested 7Â±2 for the Development Team. The 2020 guide changed this to 10 or fewer for the whole Scrum Team.
explanation.examTip: Scrum Team size: 10 or fewer total. Too small = insufficient skills. Too large = coordination overhead and complexity. The whole team including SM and PO.

questions.questionText: What does it mean for a Scrum Team to be cross-functional?

options.text: Team members can work across multiple Scrum Teams simultaneously
The team has all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint without depending on people outside the team
Each team member must be able to perform every role in the team
The team works across multiple business functions and departments

explanation.correct: Cross-functional means the team collectively has all the skills needed to create a Done Increment each Sprint â€” design, development, testing, etc. â€” without needing external help.
explanation.incorrect: Cross-functional refers to team capability, not multi-team assignment or requiring each person to do everything.
explanation.examTip: Cross-functional = team has all skills needed. Self-managing = team decides HOW to do the work. Both describe the Developers in Scrum.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Master notices that the Product Owner is frequently absent from Sprint Planning and leaves the Developers to self-direct without a clear Sprint Goal. Developers are unsure what to focus on.
questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Take over the Product Owner's responsibilities until they become available
Coach the Product Owner on the importance of their active participation and the impact their absence has on the team's ability to create value
Allow the Developers to determine their own Sprint Goal without the Product Owner
Cancel the Sprint until the Product Owner is available

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by helping them understand their accountability. Coaching the PO on their critical role in Sprint Planning and the Sprint Goal is the appropriate servant-leader action.
explanation.incorrect: SM taking over PO responsibilities blurs accountability. Developers without a PO-defined Sprint Goal leads to misaligned work. Sprint cancellation is only done by PO when Sprint Goal is obsolete.
explanation.examTip: SM's response to dysfunction = coach, not take over. When PO is absent, the SM helps the PO understand what they're missing, not replaces them.

questions.questionText: What is the Product Goal in Scrum?

options.text: The business objective that the current sprint aims to achieve
The long-term objective for the Scrum Team that the Product Backlog describes a path toward
The target release date for the next major product version
The acceptance criteria for the most important Product Backlog item

explanation.correct: The Product Goal is the commitment for the Product Backlog â€” it describes the future state of the product and serves as a long-term objective for the Scrum Team to plan against.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint Goal = sprint-level objective. Product Goal = product-level long-term objective. It is not a date or acceptance criteria.
explanation.examTip: Product Backlog â†’ committed to Product Goal. Sprint Backlog â†’ committed to Sprint Goal. Increment â†’ committed to Definition of Done.

questions.questionText: What is Product Backlog refinement?

options.text: A mandatory Scrum event that must occur at the start of each sprint
The ongoing activity of adding detail, estimates, and ordering to Product Backlog items
The final review of all product backlog items before the product is released
The process of removing completed items from the Product Backlog

explanation.correct: Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing collaborative activity where the Scrum Team adds detail, estimates, and ordering to Product Backlog items â€” not a formal Scrum event, but recommended practice.
explanation.incorrect: Refinement is not a mandatory Scrum event (the five events are Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective). It's an ongoing activity.
explanation.examTip: Refinement is NOT one of the 5 Scrum events â€” it's a continuous activity. Usually consumes no more than 10% of the team's capacity.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Scrum roles and accountabilities.

statements.text: The Scrum Master may serve as a facilitator for Scrum events.
The Product Owner can delegate Product Backlog management to the Developers.
Developers are self-managing and decide how to accomplish sprint work.
The Scrum Master assigns tasks to individual Developers during Sprint Planning.

explanation.correct: SM facilitates events. Developers self-manage (decide how). PO may work with others but remains accountable for the backlog â€” delegation doesn't remove accountability. SM never assigns tasks.
explanation.incorrect: PO remains accountable for backlog even if they delegate tasks. SM assigns tasks = command-and-control, not servant leadership.
explanation.examTip: Developers are self-managing: they choose their own work, estimate their own stories, and decide how to build. No one tells them how to do technical work.

questions.scenarioText: A company has assigned both the Scrum Master and Product Owner roles to the same person. This person is also managing the project budget.
questions.questionText: What is the problem with this arrangement?

options.text: There is no problem â€” the Scrum Guide does not prohibit combining roles
Combining the PO and SM roles creates a conflict of interest â€” the PO focuses on maximising value while the SM serves the team, and combining them undermines both accountabilities
The problem is budget management â€” financial roles should always be separate
The team size is too small â€” a dedicated developer is needed instead

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide discourages combining PO and SM roles as it creates a conflict of interest â€” the PO makes decisions about what to build and the SM facilitates the team's process. Combining them undermines the checks and balances.
explanation.incorrect: The Scrum Guide specifically notes that the SM and PO should not be the same person, as it creates a conflict. Budget management is a separate concern.
explanation.examTip: PO + SM conflict: PO wants max value (pushes team), SM protects team process (serves team). Same person serving both pulls in opposite directions.

questions.questionText: Who is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: The Product Owner creates it based on priorities
The Scrum Master creates it to organise the team's work
The Developers create it during Sprint Planning
It is created collaboratively by the entire Scrum Team including stakeholders

explanation.correct: The Sprint Backlog is created by the Developers during Sprint Planning. It consists of the Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering the Increment.
explanation.incorrect: PO is accountable for the Product Backlog, not Sprint Backlog. SM facilitates but doesn't create it. Stakeholders don't participate in creating the Sprint Backlog.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Backlog = owned by Developers. Product Backlog = owned by PO. Developers can update the Sprint Backlog throughout the sprint as they learn more.

questions.scenarioText: A senior developer tells the Scrum Master that they believe they should be exempt from the Daily Scrum because they are highly experienced and find the meetings unproductive.
questions.questionText: How should the Scrum Master respond?

options.text: Grant the exemption â€” senior developers shouldn't need to attend
Explain that the Daily Scrum is for all Developers and explore why they find it unproductive, then help the team improve how they run it
Report the developer's attitude to the Product Owner for resolution
Make attendance mandatory and increase the Daily Scrum duration to ensure all issues are covered

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master's role is to coach and serve. The appropriate response is to understand the developer's concern (maybe the Daily Scrum is run poorly), and help the team improve the event's effectiveness.
explanation.incorrect: No exemptions â€” Daily Scrum is for all Developers. Reporting to PO bypasses SM responsibility. Making it longer contradicts the 15-minute timebox principle.
explanation.examTip: SM response to dysfunction = curiosity and coaching. 'Why is it unproductive?' is the right first question. Maybe the event needs to change, not the attendance requirement.

questions.questionText: What does the Increment represent at the end of a Sprint?

options.text: The total list of features planned for the current release
The sum of all Product Backlog items completed during the sprint and all previous sprints, meeting the Definition of Done
The features demonstrated at the Sprint Review
The stories completed in the current sprint only

explanation.correct: The Increment is cumulative â€” it is the sum of all completed PBIs from the current sprint PLUS all previous sprints, each meeting the Definition of Done. Each sprint adds to the overall product.
explanation.incorrect: The Increment is cumulative (all sprints), not just the current sprint. The Sprint Review demonstrates the Increment but doesn't define it.
explanation.examTip: Increment = all Done work this sprint + all previous sprints' Done work. Must be in a usable condition and meet DoD. May or may not be released.

questions.scenarioText: A stakeholder requests that the Scrum Team work on an urgent feature that was not in the Sprint Backlog. The stakeholder goes directly to a Developer and asks them to start on it immediately.
questions.questionText: What is the correct response?

options.text: The Developer should start work on the urgent feature to maintain stakeholder satisfaction
The Developer should redirect the stakeholder to the Product Owner, who evaluates the urgency and decides whether to adjust the Sprint or add it to the Product Backlog
The Scrum Master should reject the request as it violates the Sprint Backlog
The whole team should vote on whether to accept the new work

explanation.correct: The Product Owner is the single authority on what the team works on. Stakeholders should direct requests to the PO, who evaluates urgency and decides whether to add to the Product Backlog or address current sprint.
explanation.incorrect: Developers should not accept work directly from stakeholders (bypasses PO). SM's role is not to reject but to help redirect. Team vote on ad-hoc work undermines PO authority.
explanation.examTip: All new work requests â†’ Product Owner. PO decides priority. Developers protect Sprint Goal. No one else can add work to the Sprint without PO involvement.

questions.questionText: What does it mean that the Scrum Team is self-managing?

options.text: The team manages itself without any oversight from the organisation
The Scrum Team internally decides who does what, when, and how
Each team member manages their own individual tasks independently
The team can hire and fire its own members

explanation.correct: Self-managing means the Scrum Team (specifically the Developers) internally decides who does what, when, and how â€” without being directed by people outside the team. They are given a problem to solve, not a prescriptive plan.
explanation.incorrect: Self-managing doesn't mean unaccountable to the organisation. It applies to how work is done, not HR decisions. It's a team property, not individual.
explanation.examTip: Self-managing Developers: choose which stories to work on, decide technical approaches, self-assign tasks. No external person tells Developers how to do their technical work.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it is consistent with the Scrum Guide.

statements.text: The Scrum Master must be a full-time role and cannot do other work.
The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
Developers may not change the Sprint Backlog once the Sprint has started.
Each Scrum Team should have its own Product Owner and Scrum Master.

explanation.correct: PO is one person (not committee). Each Scrum Team has its own PO and SM. SM can do other work. Developers update Sprint Backlog throughout the sprint as they learn more.
explanation.incorrect: SM full-time = not required by Scrum Guide. Immutable Sprint Backlog = not Scrum â€” Developers adapt their plan throughout the sprint.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Backlog evolves during sprint. Developers update it daily as they gain new information. It's a living plan, not a fixed contract.

questions.questionText: Who should attend the Sprint Review?

options.text: Only the Scrum Team
The Scrum Team and key stakeholders invited by the Product Owner
All stakeholders, management, and the Scrum Team
Only the Developers â€” stakeholders distract from the review

explanation.correct: The Sprint Review is attended by the Scrum Team plus key stakeholders invited by the Product Owner. Stakeholder participation is essential â€” their feedback informs future Product Backlog decisions.
explanation.incorrect: The Sprint Review requires stakeholders to be useful. All stakeholders/management is too broad. Developers alone defeats the purpose of stakeholder feedback.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review attendees: Scrum Team + stakeholders (invited by PO). The goal is collaborative discussion about the product, not a demo presentation.

questions.scenarioText: A team has been working in Scrum for 6 months. The manager wants to add a senior developer from another team to help with the next sprint without consulting the Scrum Team.
questions.questionText: How should the Scrum Master respond?

options.text: Accept the addition â€” more developers will increase velocity
Explain that changing team composition mid-sprint disrupts the team and invite discussion about timing and team needs
Tell the manager that only the Product Owner can make personnel decisions
Ask the new developer to attend the Daily Scrum immediately to integrate

explanation.correct: The SM protects the team from disruptions. Adding people mid-sprint disrupts the team's dynamics and established Sprint Backlog commitments. The SM should explain the impact and facilitate a proper discussion.
explanation.incorrect: More developers don't automatically increase sprint velocity (Brooks' Law). PO doesn't control HR. Immediate integration ignores the disruption impact.
explanation.examTip: Brooks' Law: 'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.' Team changes ideally happen between sprints. SM protects team from external disruptions.

questions.questionText: Can the Product Owner order (prioritise) the Product Backlog based on factors other than business value?

options.text: No â€” the Product Backlog must always be ordered by business value alone
Yes â€” the PO may order the backlog using any combination of factors including risk, dependencies, learning, and strategic value
Yes â€” but only with approval from the Scrum Master
No â€” ordering is determined by stakeholder votes

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide says the PO orders the Product Backlog to best achieve goals and missions. Ordering factors can include business value, risk reduction, learning, technical dependencies, regulatory requirements, and more.
explanation.incorrect: Business value alone is too limiting. The PO doesn't need SM approval for backlog ordering. Stakeholder votes don't determine ordering â€” PO does.
explanation.examTip: PO owns backlog ordering. The Scrum Guide uses 'ordered' not 'prioritised' â€” because priority implies only value, but ordering considers many factors.

questions.scenarioText: During a sprint, the Developers discover that the work is more complex than estimated and they will not complete all selected Product Backlog items. The Scrum Master suggests adding more items to the Sprint Backlog to keep the team busy.
questions.questionText: Is this appropriate?

options.text: Yes â€” the team should always be working at full capacity
No â€” the Developers should focus on the Sprint Goal. They may negotiate scope with the PO, or reduce scope to protect the Sprint Goal
Yes â€” the Scrum Master should add items to motivate the team
No â€” the sprint should be cancelled and replanned with more accurate estimates

explanation.correct: When capacity is insufficient, Developers should focus on the Sprint Goal. They may negotiate scope (remove less critical items) with the PO to protect the Sprint Goal, rather than adding more work.
explanation.incorrect: Adding more work when struggling makes things worse. SM doesn't add items to Sprint Backlog. Cancellation is only for obsolete Sprint Goals.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Goal is the commitment â€” protect it. Items selected are the plan. If the plan is wrong, adjust items but protect the Sprint Goal.

questions.questionText: Match each Scrum artifact to its associated commitment.

explanation.correct: Each Scrum artifact has a commitment: Product Backlog â†’ Product Goal (long-term objective), Sprint Backlog â†’ Sprint Goal (sprint objective), Increment â†’ Definition of Done (quality standard).
explanation.incorrect: These commitments were formalised in the 2020 Scrum Guide. They enhance transparency and create focus.
explanation.examTip: Artifactâ€“Commitment pairs: Product Backlog/Product Goal, Sprint Backlog/Sprint Goal, Increment/DoD. This is a key 2020 Scrum Guide addition.

questions.questionText: What is the Scrum Master's responsibility regarding impediments?

options.text: To document all impediments and report them to management weekly
To cause the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress
To assign impediments to individual Developers to resolve
To prevent impediments from arising by planning the sprint thoroughly

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master causes the removal of impediments â€” they may remove them directly if within their authority, or escalate/coordinate with others. The key word is 'causes' â€” they don't always personally remove every impediment.
explanation.incorrect: Reporting to management is one mechanism but not the full accountability. SM doesn't assign impediments to Devs. Sprint planning can't prevent all impediments.
explanation.examTip: SM causes impediment removal â€” sometimes directly, sometimes by escalating to others who have authority. Key: they own the process, not just awareness.

questions.questionText: In Scrum, who is allowed to make changes to the Sprint Backlog during a Sprint?

options.text: Only the Product Owner
Only the Scrum Master
Only the Developers
Any member of the Scrum Team

explanation.correct: The Sprint Backlog is owned by the Developers â€” they are the only ones who can change it during a Sprint. The PO and SM do not modify the Sprint Backlog.
explanation.incorrect: PO owns Product Backlog. SM facilitates. Only Developers modify the Sprint Backlog.
explanation.examTip: Product Backlog â†’ PO owns. Sprint Backlog â†’ Developers own. Only the owner modifies their backlog.

questions.scenarioText: The Scrum Team's stakeholders are unhappy because they receive no visibility into the team's work until the Sprint Review. They want daily progress reports.
questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Agree to provide daily written reports to all stakeholders
Help stakeholders understand Scrum's transparency mechanisms (task board, burndown, Sprint Review) and invite them to engage with the Product Owner for updates
Ask the Product Owner to attend meetings with stakeholders every day
Invite all stakeholders to the Daily Scrum

explanation.correct: The SM helps stakeholders understand how Scrum provides transparency. Information radiators (boards, burndowns), regular PO engagement, and Sprint Reviews are the Scrum mechanisms for visibility â€” not daily reports.
explanation.incorrect: Daily reports create overhead without Scrum value. Daily PO stakeholder meetings are unsustainable. Stakeholders attending Daily Scrum disrupts the Developers' self-management event.
explanation.examTip: Scrum transparency tools: Product Backlog (visible to all), Sprint Backlog (visible to team), burndown charts, information radiators, Sprint Review. Stakeholders don't attend Daily Scrum.

questions.questionText: What is the Scrum Team's primary objective?

options.text: To complete all items in the Sprint Backlog every Sprint
To create a valuable, useful Increment each Sprint that moves toward the Product Goal
To meet the velocity targets set by management
To deliver the entire product within the agreed-upon schedule

explanation.correct: The Scrum Team exists to deliver value. Their primary objective is to create a valuable, useful Increment each Sprint that makes progress toward the Product Goal â€” not just to complete a list of tasks.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint Backlog completion is a means, not the goal. Velocity targets are a management anti-pattern. Scrum is iterative, not a fixed schedule.
explanation.examTip: Scrum is about value delivery, not task completion. A team that completes all sprint tasks but delivers no value has failed the sprint's purpose.

questions.questionText: What is meant by the term 'done' in Scrum?

options.text: The Developer has finished coding the feature
The Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done and is part of a usable Increment
The Product Owner has accepted the story
All tasks on the Sprint Backlog have been completed

explanation.correct: 'Done' means the Product Backlog item meets every criterion in the Definition of Done and can be included in a usable, releasable Increment.
explanation.incorrect: Coding alone is not done. PO acceptance is part of the Review but not the definition of done. Task completion is a means, not the measure of done.
explanation.examTip: Done = meets DoD. Not: 'I finished coding', 'PO approved it', 'tasks are complete'. The DoD is the only criterion.

questions.scenarioText: A new Scrum Team has no organisational Definition of Done. During their first Sprint Planning, they are unsure what standards to apply to their work.
questions.questionText: What should they do?

options.text: Skip the Definition of Done and define it after the first sprint once they understand the work better
The Scrum Team should create their own Definition of Done appropriate for their product before the first Sprint begins
The Scrum Master should create a standard Definition of Done for the organisation
The Product Owner defines the DoD based on business acceptance criteria

explanation.correct: When no organisational DoD exists, the Scrum Team must create one that is appropriate for their product. The DoD must exist before work begins to ensure transparency and quality from the start.
explanation.incorrect: DoD cannot be skipped â€” work without a DoD has no quality standard. SM doesn't create it alone. PO doesn't own it â€” the whole Scrum Team creates it.
explanation.examTip: DoD ownership: if the organisation has one, teams must follow it (and can strengthen it). If not, the Scrum Team creates their own. It's a whole-team commitment.

questions.questionText: How should a Scrum Team handle undone work at the end of a Sprint?

options.text: Include it in the Increment and note it as 'partially complete'
Return it to the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to re-evaluate and potentially include in a future Sprint
Carry it forward to the next Sprint automatically
The Scrum Master marks it as done and closes the sprint

explanation.correct: Undone items cannot be included in the Increment (they don't meet the DoD). They return to the Product Backlog where the PO re-evaluates their order and decides when to address them.
explanation.incorrect: Partial Increments violate the DoD. Auto-carry-forward bypasses PO's re-prioritisation authority. SM cannot mark items done.
explanation.examTip: Undone work â†’ Product Backlog. PO re-estimates and re-orders. Developers re-estimate for next sprint if selected. Don't auto-carry-over.

questions.scenarioText: The Scrum Team has been using Scrum for 3 sprints. Management insists the team provide a detailed project plan with tasks, deadlines, and resource allocation for the next 6 months.
questions.questionText: How should the Scrum Master respond?

options.text: Create the 6-month plan as requested to maintain management support
Help management understand how Scrum provides planning through the Product Backlog, Sprint Planning, and release forecasting while explaining why detailed long-term plans have low value
Ask the Product Owner to create the plan since they own the backlog
Refuse and explain that Scrum does not allow any planning beyond the current sprint

explanation.correct: The SM serves the organisation by coaching leadership on Scrum. They should help management understand how Scrum provides predictability (Product Backlog, velocity, release forecasts) while explaining the empirical nature of complex work.
explanation.incorrect: Creating a detailed 6-month plan contradicts empiricism. PO doesn't own long-range planning alone. Scrum doesn't prohibit all planning â€” the Product Backlog IS a plan.
explanation.examTip: SM coaches management: Product Backlog = roadmap, velocity = forecast, Sprint = short-term plan. Long-term detailed plans are false precision in complex work.

questions.questionText: What is the key characteristic that distinguishes a Scrum Master as a 'servant leader'?

options.text: They work without pay and volunteer their services
They put the needs of the team and organisation first, supporting and enabling others to succeed rather than directing and controlling
They take on the lowest-priority tasks the team doesn't want to do
They manage the team's work and assign tasks while remaining humble

explanation.correct: Servant leadership means prioritising the growth and well-being of the team and organisation â€” the SM empowers others, removes obstacles, and facilitates rather than directing, commanding, or managing.
explanation.incorrect: Servant leadership is a leadership philosophy, not about unpaid work or task assignment. SM does not assign tasks.
explanation.examTip: Servant leader: empowers others, removes impediments, facilitates, coaches. NOT: commands, assigns tasks, manages output. The team is the priority.

questions.questionText: In Scrum, who is responsible for maximising value?

options.text: The Scrum Master, through effective facilitation
The Product Owner, through effective Product Backlog management
The Developers, through high-quality technical delivery
The whole Scrum Team equally

explanation.correct: The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product and the work of the Scrum Team. They do this through effective Product Backlog management â€” ordering, detailing, and communicating items.
explanation.incorrect: While everyone contributes to value, the PO is specifically accountable for maximising it. SM optimises the process. Developers deliver quality.
explanation.examTip: PO = accountable for WHAT is built and in what order = value maximisation. SM = accountable for HOW the team works. Devs = accountable for quality of the Increment.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team is finishing a sprint. Three stories were completed and meet the Definition of Done. Two stories were started but not finished. The Product Owner wants to present all five stories at the Sprint Review as 'mostly done'.
questions.questionText: What should happen at the Sprint Review?

options.text: Present all five stories as the Product Owner requested â€” partial progress is still valuable to show
Only present the three completed stories that meet the DoD as the Increment. The two unfinished stories are not part of the Increment.
Cancel the Sprint Review since not all work is complete
Present all five stories but label the unfinished ones as 'in progress'

explanation.correct: Only work that meets the Definition of Done is part of the Increment and can be presented at the Sprint Review. Presenting unfinished work as 'mostly done' violates transparency â€” a core Scrum pillar.
explanation.incorrect: Presenting incomplete work as part of the Increment undermines transparency and quality. Sprint Review is not cancelled due to incomplete items.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review = inspect the Increment (Done work only). Undone work â‰  Increment. Transparency requires showing the real state.

questions.questionText: Can the Scrum Master attend the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: No â€” the Retrospective is only for Developers to discuss technical improvements
Yes â€” the Scrum Master participates as a peer team member accountable for the Scrum process
Only if the Developers invite them
Yes, but only as an observer, not as a participant

explanation.correct: The Sprint Retrospective is for the entire Scrum Team â€” Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Developers. The SM participates as a peer and often facilitates the event.
explanation.incorrect: The Retrospective is not Developers-only. The SM is a full participant. The PO also attends.
explanation.examTip: All Scrum Team members attend the Retrospective. SM often facilitates. PO attends too (but must be open to feedback). It covers people, relationships, processes, and tools.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: Product Backlog is short-term; Sprint Backlog is long-term
Product Backlog is an ordered list of all work for the product; Sprint Backlog is the team's plan for the current sprint
Product Backlog is owned by the team; Sprint Backlog is owned by the PO
They are identical but used at different levels of the organisation

explanation.correct: Product Backlog = ordered list of all desired work for the product (long-term, PO-owned, always evolving). Sprint Backlog = the Sprint Goal + selected PBIs + plan for the current sprint (Developers-owned, sprint-duration).
explanation.incorrect: The Product Backlog is long-term; Sprint Backlog is for the current sprint. Ownership is the reverse of option C.
explanation.examTip: Product Backlog: long-term, PO owns, always exists. Sprint Backlog: sprint-duration, Developers own, created in Sprint Planning, discarded at sprint end.

questions.scenarioText: During a Sprint, a Developer raises a technical issue in the Daily Scrum. The discussion becomes extended and consumes most of the 15-minute timebox.
questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Extend the Daily Scrum to ensure the technical issue is fully resolved
Note the topic and suggest a follow-up meeting with the relevant Developers after the Daily Scrum
Ask the Developer to raise the issue in the Sprint Review instead
Add the technical issue to the Product Backlog for future consideration

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum is time-boxed to 15 minutes for inspection and planning. Technical discussions are taken 'offline' in a follow-up meeting with only the relevant Developers â€” keeping the Daily Scrum focused and short.
explanation.incorrect: Extending violates the timebox. Sprint Review is not the place for technical discussions. Technical issues during development are not Product Backlog items.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum = 15 min max, inspect Sprint Goal progress. Extended discussions = after the event, subset of relevant people. SM ensures timebox is respected.

questions.questionText: What is the relationship between the Sprint Goal and the selected Product Backlog items?

options.text: The Sprint Goal is derived from the selected PBIs â€” it summarises what will be built
The Sprint Goal provides coherence and flexibility â€” selected PBIs serve the Sprint Goal, but the Goal can be met even if not all PBIs are completed
They are independent â€” Sprint Goal describes business value, PBIs describe technical work
Completing all selected PBIs automatically achieves the Sprint Goal

explanation.correct: The Sprint Goal is the objective. The selected PBIs are the plan to achieve it. Developers have flexibility in implementation â€” if a better approach is found during the sprint, they can adjust the PBIs while still meeting the Sprint Goal.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint Goal comes first (why), then PBIs are selected (what). They are related but the Goal survives even if the plan changes. Not all PBIs completing doesn't necessarily mean the Goal is unmet.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Goal = commitment. PBIs = implementation plan. Goal gives flexibility â€” Developers can adapt HOW they achieve the goal during the sprint.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team has multiple Product Owners â€” one for each major area of the product. Each PO manages their own Product Backlog and the Developers work from multiple backlogs simultaneously.
questions.questionText: What is wrong with this arrangement?

options.text: Nothing â€” having multiple Product Owners is an efficient way to scale Scrum
Each Scrum Team must have one Product Owner who is solely accountable for one ordered Product Backlog
The problem is the multiple backlogs â€” they should be merged into one
Multiple POs are fine as long as the Scrum Master coordinates between them

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide is explicit: one Product Owner per Scrum Team, one Product Backlog per Scrum Team. Multiple POs create conflicting priorities and confuse the team about who owns value decisions.
explanation.incorrect: Multiple POs violates the Scrum Guide. The issue is both the multiple POs AND the multiple backlogs â€” both must be singular.
explanation.examTip: One Scrum Team = one PO + one Product Backlog. For large products with multiple teams, frameworks like LeSS and SAFe provide scaling solutions with one PO and one backlog.

questions.questionText: What is an anti-pattern in Scrum?

options.text: A pattern that is against Scrum best practices and undermines its effectiveness
A design pattern used in software development
A team pattern that happens rarely and is considered unusual
A pattern used in the retrospective to identify improvements

explanation.correct: A Scrum anti-pattern is a commonly observed behaviour or practice that appears reasonable but undermines Scrum's effectiveness â€” such as skipping retrospectives, allowing the SM to assign tasks, or having the PO absent from sprint events.
explanation.incorrect: Anti-pattern is a specific term meaning a counter-productive practice, not software design, rarity, or retrospective format.
explanation.examTip: Common Scrum anti-patterns: Sprint 0 (no increment), hardening sprints, SM assigning tasks, PO absent from events, skipping retrospectives, treating Scrum events as overhead.

questions.scenarioText: A company wants to use Scrum but plans to have Sprints with no Sprint Reviews or Retrospectives to save time. They call this 'Scrum Lite'.
questions.questionText: What is the problem with this approach?

options.text: There is no problem â€” teams can customise Scrum to their needs
Removing events from Scrum makes it incomplete â€” you cannot call it Scrum if the prescribed events are removed
The problem is only the name â€” calling it something else would make it acceptable
Sprint Reviews can be skipped but Retrospectives must be kept

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide states Scrum is immutable â€” you may find value in using only parts of it, but that is not Scrum. Removing inspection/adaptation events (Review, Retro) eliminates empiricism, which is Scrum's foundation.
explanation.incorrect: Scrum cannot be partially followed and still called Scrum. Renaming doesn't fix the missing empirical process. Both events are required.
explanation.examTip: Scrum Guide: 'Scrum's rules are designed to be a whole. If you remove or change parts of Scrum, you are not doing Scrum.' You may still get value, but don't call it Scrum.

questions.questionText: What does the Scrum Guide say about the Sprint length consistency?

options.text: Sprint lengths should vary based on workload
Sprints should be consistent in length â€” changing sprint length too frequently undermines predictability
Each sprint can have a different length as long as it is agreed in Sprint Planning
Sprint length must be reviewed and agreed by management each quarter

explanation.correct: Sprint length should be consistent â€” using the same length creates a cadence that establishes a heartbeat for the team and organisation, improving predictability and planning.
explanation.incorrect: Variable sprint lengths undermine cadence and predictability. Sprint length is a team decision, not a management one.
explanation.examTip: Same sprint length = consistent cadence = predictability. Changing sprint length too often resets the team's rhythm. Once chosen, keep it stable.

questions.scenarioText: The Developers are 3 days into a 2-week sprint. They realise the Sprint Goal is no longer achievable because a key dependency â€” an external API â€” will not be available in time.
questions.questionText: What should the team do?

options.text: Continue as planned and deliver whatever is possible at sprint end
Raise the impediment to the Scrum Master immediately and work with the Product Owner to renegotiate the Sprint Goal or select alternative PBIs
Cancel the sprint â€” the Sprint Goal is no longer achievable
Move the dependency to the next sprint's backlog and work on other tasks

explanation.correct: When new information makes the Sprint Goal unachievable, the team should raise the impediment immediately. The SM helps remove it and the PO works with Developers to adapt â€” potentially modifying the Sprint Goal or selecting different PBIs.
explanation.incorrect: Continuing with an unachievable goal wastes effort. Only the PO can cancel a sprint (Sprint Goal must be obsolete, not just difficult). Silently moving work away doesn't address the problem.
explanation.examTip: New information during sprint = raise immediately, inspect, adapt. SM removes impediment. PO and Devs renegotiate scope or Sprint Goal if necessary.

questions.questionText: Can the Product Owner be a member of the Developers in the same Scrum Team?

options.text: Yes, always â€” the PO must understand the technical work
Yes, but this may lead to conflicts of interest and is discouraged
No â€” the PO is never allowed to do development work
Yes, this is the recommended setup for small teams

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide doesn't explicitly prohibit the PO from doing development work, but doing so leads to conflicts between their PO accountability (ordering the backlog, maximising value) and their Developer role (doing the work).
explanation.incorrect: Being both PO and Developer creates conflicts of interest. It's not recommended but not explicitly prohibited by the Scrum Guide.
explanation.examTip: PO as Developer = conflict of interest. Who decides what to build when you're both the decider and the builder? Generally discouraged in practice.

questions.questionText: Place the steps of Sprint Planning in the correct order.

orderItems.text: Discuss why the sprint is valuable (Sprint Goal)
Select Product Backlog items to work on
Decompose selected items into tasks and plan how to create the Increment
Finalise and commit to the Sprint Backlog

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning order: Why (Sprint Goal) â†’ What (select PBIs) â†’ How (decompose into tasks, plan delivery) â†’ Sprint Backlog commitment.
explanation.incorrect: The 'why' (Sprint Goal) always comes first. Selection before decomposition. Commitment happens at the end after full planning.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Planning three topics in order: Why (value/Sprint Goal) â†’ What (which PBIs) â†’ How (plan/tasks). Output = Sprint Backlog.

questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do if the Scrum Team is consistently not meeting the Definition of Done?

options.text: Lower the Definition of Done to match what the team can achieve
Help the team identify root causes and coach them on improving their technical practices and engineering skills
Report the quality issues to management and request replacement team members
Ask the Product Owner to remove quality criteria from the DoD

explanation.correct: The SM coaches the team toward technical excellence. Consistently missing DoD = a systemic issue (missing skills, practices, or time). The SM facilitates improvement through coaching, retrospectives, and potentially bringing in technical coaches.
explanation.incorrect: Lowering DoD hides the problem and ships lower quality. Management escalation bypasses team ownership. Removing quality criteria from DoD defeats its purpose.
explanation.examTip: DoD should become more stringent over time, not less. If team can't meet DoD, address root cause: skills gaps, technical debt, insufficient testing time.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it is true according to the Scrum Guide.

statements.text: An Increment must be released to end users at the end of every Sprint.
Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint.
The Increment must be in a usable condition even if the Product Owner decides not to release it.
The decision to release the Increment is made by the Developers.

explanation.correct: Multiple Increments can be created per sprint. The Increment must be usable (meets DoD) regardless of whether it's released. The PO decides release timing, not Developers. Releasing every sprint is not mandatory.
explanation.incorrect: Release is PO's decision. Increment usability (DoD) is mandatory but release is optional. Multiple Increments per sprint = allowed and encouraged.
explanation.examTip: Increment = usable, Done. Release decision = PO. Multiple Increments per sprint possible. Sprint end Increment â‰  must release.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team has been working well for several sprints. A Developer approaches the Scrum Master privately to say they believe another Developer is not contributing fairly and should be removed from the team.
questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Remove the underperforming Developer from the team as requested
Coach the team to address interpersonal issues directly through the Retrospective and encourage the concerned Developer to raise the issue openly with the team
Keep the conversation confidential and monitor the situation without action
Inform the Product Owner and let them decide on team composition

explanation.correct: The SM fosters a collaborative environment where teams resolve issues themselves. Coaching the concerned Developer to raise the issue in the Retrospective or directly with the team enables the self-managing team to address it appropriately.
explanation.incorrect: SM cannot remove team members. Confidential inaction ignores a team dynamic issue. PO doesn't manage team composition in self-managing teams.
explanation.examTip: Team conflict = coach team to self-manage. Retrospective is the right venue for team dynamic issues. SM enables, not resolves, team conflicts directly.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of the Scrum Master serving the organisation?

options.text: Writing user stories for the Product Owner
Coaching leadership on how to support empirical product development and self-managing teams
Managing the organisation's project portfolio
Reporting team velocity to management every week

explanation.correct: The SM serves the organisation by coaching leadership on Scrum adoption, helping remove organisational impediments, and guiding how to interact with Scrum Teams to enable empirical product development.
explanation.incorrect: Writing user stories = serving PO (not the right way). Portfolio management = outside SM scope. Velocity reporting doesn't help the organisation understand Scrum.
explanation.examTip: SM serves 3 entities: Developers (coaching, impediment removal), PO (backlog help, stakeholder guidance), Organisation (leadership coaching, Scrum adoption).

questions.scenarioText: After 4 sprints, the Scrum Team's velocity has been inconsistent: 30, 15, 40, 20 story points. Management is concerned and asks the Scrum Master to investigate.
questions.questionText: What is the BEST explanation for this pattern and what should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: The team is underperforming â€” increase sprint length to improve consistency
Velocity variation is normal early in team formation. The SM should help the team identify factors causing inconsistency (estimation, impediments, team stability) through retrospectives
Velocity should be fixed by management and enforced as a team target
The team should switch to hours-based tracking instead of story points

explanation.correct: Velocity varies naturally, especially early on. The SM coaches the team to investigate root causes (poor estimation, impediments, scope changes, team instability) through retrospectives â€” not through management control.
explanation.incorrect: Velocity is an empirical measure, not a target. Management-enforced velocity = pressure to cut corners. Switching to hours doesn't solve underlying issues.
explanation.examTip: Velocity = planning tool, not a performance metric. Consistent velocity develops over time with team stability. Use it to forecast, not to judge the team.

questions.questionText: What makes Scrum different from traditional project management approaches?

options.text: Scrum eliminates all planning and documentation
Scrum uses iterative, incremental delivery with frequent inspect-and-adapt cycles rather than sequential phases with fixed plans
Scrum only works for software development projects
Scrum has no roles or responsibilities â€” the team is entirely self-governing

explanation.correct: Scrum's core differentiator is its iterative-incremental approach combined with empiricism â€” frequent short cycles with inspect-and-adapt, rather than sequential phases (requirements â†’ design â†’ build â†’ test) with upfront fixed planning.
explanation.incorrect: Scrum has planning (Sprint Planning, Product Backlog) and documentation (Sprint Backlog, Increment). Scrum works beyond software. It has well-defined roles.
explanation.examTip: Scrum vs waterfall: iterative vs sequential, empirical vs plan-driven, adaptive vs fixed. Scrum acknowledges complexity; waterfall assumes predictability.

questions.scenarioText: During Sprint Planning, the Product Owner presents the top items in the Product Backlog but they are large and vague. Developers cannot confidently estimate or commit to the Sprint Goal.
questions.questionText: What should happen?

options.text: Developers should estimate based on the information available and adjust later
Sprint Planning should proceed with whatever items are ready; unready items should remain in the Product Backlog for refinement before the next sprint
The Scrum Master should write the missing details during Sprint Planning
Cancel Sprint Planning and hold a backlog refinement session instead

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning should only pull items the team can confidently commit to. Unrefined items stay in the Product Backlog. This outcome reinforces the need for regular refinement before Sprint Planning.
explanation.incorrect: Committing to vague items leads to sprint failure. SM doesn't write requirements. Sprint Planning is a Scrum event and should not be cancelled.
explanation.examTip: Unrefined backlog = sprint planning problem. Solution: only pull ready items, and use the lesson to improve the refinement process before next Sprint Planning.

questions.questionText: What does it mean for the Scrum Team to be focused?

options.text: Everyone must work on a single task until it is complete
The Scrum Team focuses their work on the Sprint Goal and making progress toward the Product Goal each sprint
Team members should not be distracted by anything outside their sprint tasks
The team focuses on completing as many items as possible each sprint

explanation.correct: Focus as a Scrum value means the Scrum Team focuses on the Sprint Goal and making progress toward the Product Goal â€” not maximising story points or rigid single-tasking.
explanation.incorrect: Focus is a value about purposeful direction (Sprint Goal/Product Goal), not strict single-tasking or isolation from the world.
explanation.examTip: 5 Scrum values in action: Focus (Sprint Goal), Commitment (to goals), Courage (difficult conversations), Openness (about work), Respect (for each other).

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team delivers a product used by multiple business units. Each business unit believes their needs should be the top priority. The Scrum Team is pulled in multiple directions each sprint.
questions.questionText: What is the BEST solution?

options.text: Create separate sprint backlogs for each business unit
Ensure there is one Product Owner who takes input from all business units and makes the final prioritisation decisions for one unified Product Backlog
Let each business unit send a representative to Sprint Planning to negotiate priorities
Split the Scrum Team into sub-teams for each business unit

explanation.correct: One Product Owner with one Product Backlog is fundamental to Scrum. The PO integrates all stakeholder needs and makes the final ordering decision â€” eliminating competing priorities and giving the team a single, clear direction.
explanation.incorrect: Multiple backlogs create competing priorities. Negotiation by multiple parties in Sprint Planning violates PO authority. Splitting teams per business unit creates coordination overhead and may not be optimal.
explanation.examTip: Multiple stakeholders â†’ one PO to mediate. PO's job is to balance competing priorities into a single ordered backlog. This is the core value the PO provides.

questions.questionText: What does 'openness' as a Scrum value mean in practice?

options.text: The team's code repository must be publicly accessible
The Scrum Team and stakeholders are open about all the work and challenges they face
Team members must share their personal goals and challenges in the Daily Scrum
The Product Backlog must be visible to all employees in the organisation

explanation.correct: Openness in Scrum means the team and stakeholders are transparent about the work, progress, learnings, and problems â€” sharing real status rather than presenting optimistic pictures.
explanation.incorrect: Openness is about work transparency, not public code, personal sharing, or literal backlog access by all employees.
explanation.examTip: Openness enables transparency, which enables inspection, which enables adaptation. Hiding problems = violates openness = breaks empiricism.

questions.scenarioText: An organisation has adopted Scrum but the managers continue to assign individual tasks to Developers and hold private performance reviews based on individual task completion rates.
questions.questionText: How does this conflict with Scrum?

options.text: It does not conflict â€” individual performance measurement is compatible with Scrum
It conflicts with self-management â€” task assignment and individual metrics undermine the team's ability to self-organise and make collective decisions about how to work
It only conflicts if the Scrum Master is not informed of the task assignments
Managers assigning tasks is fine â€” it speeds up the Daily Scrum

explanation.correct: Management assigning tasks to individuals bypasses the self-managing team's authority to decide how to accomplish their work. Individual metrics create incentives that conflict with team collaboration and Sprint Goal focus.
explanation.incorrect: External task assignment undermines self-management regardless of whether the SM knows. Managers directing individual work is a core Scrum anti-pattern.
explanation.examTip: Management's role changes in Scrum: from assigning work â†’ to removing impediments and supporting the team. Self-management requires trusting the team to organise their own work.

questions.questionText: What is the role of the Scrum Master in relation to the Product Owner?

options.text: The SM manages the PO and ensures they follow the Scrum process
The SM helps the PO understand and practice effective Product Backlog management and facilitates stakeholder collaboration
The SM approves backlog items before the PO can publish them
The SM has no responsibility toward the PO â€” they only serve the Developers

explanation.correct: The SM serves the PO by helping them find techniques for effective Product Backlog management, facilitating stakeholder events, and coaching them on Scrum practices.
explanation.incorrect: SM doesn't manage or approve PO work. SM serves all three entities: PO, Developers, and organisation.
explanation.examTip: SM serving PO: coaching on backlog management, facilitating events, helping communicate product vision, removing organisational impediments to PO effectiveness.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team is co-located except for one Developer who works remotely. The team struggles to include the remote Developer effectively in the Daily Scrum and Sprint events.
questions.questionText: What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Ask the remote Developer to attend all events in person for the Scrum to work properly
Facilitate the team in finding collaboration tools and working agreements that make remote participation as effective as in-person for all team members
Exclude the remote Developer from events they cannot participate in effectively
Schedule separate meetings for the remote Developer after the main team events

explanation.correct: The SM facilitates team effectiveness in whatever context they work. This means helping establish tools (video conferencing, virtual boards) and working agreements that make distributed work effective.
explanation.incorrect: Requiring in-person attendance ignores reality. Exclusion from events undermines the whole-team principle. Separate meetings create a two-tier team.
explanation.examTip: Scrum works with remote/distributed teams. SM's job is to make collaboration effective regardless of location. Distributed teams need extra SM attention on communication tools and agreements.

questions.questionText: Can stakeholders attend the Daily Scrum?

options.text: Yes â€” stakeholder visibility into daily progress is encouraged
No â€” the Daily Scrum is only for Developers; others may observe only if the Developers choose to allow it
Yes â€” the Product Owner must always attend to hear the daily update
Yes â€” the Scrum Master invites key stakeholders each week

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers. Others (SM, PO, stakeholders) are not required to attend and should not disrupt the Developers' self-management. If allowed to observe, they don't participate.
explanation.incorrect: Stakeholder attendance at Daily Scrum disrupts the team's self-management and often turns it into a status meeting. PO does not need to attend.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum participants: Developers only. SM and PO may attend but should not participate unless they are also Developers. Stakeholders = not invited.

questions.scenarioText: A team's Retrospective consistently produces action items that are never implemented. The team discusses improvements every sprint but the same issues recur.
questions.questionText: What is the BEST action for the Scrum Master?

options.text: Cancel future Retrospectives until the team shows they can implement improvements
Facilitate a retrospective on the retrospective â€” help the team understand why improvements aren't being implemented and address the root cause
Ask management to enforce the retrospective action items
Take ownership of implementing the retrospective action items personally

explanation.correct: If retrospectives aren't producing change, the SM should facilitate a meta-retrospective â€” inspecting the retrospective process itself. Root causes: action items too vague, no accountability, not added to Sprint Backlog, or organisational impediments.
explanation.incorrect: Cancelling retrospectives removes the improvement mechanism. Management enforcement undermines team ownership. SM implementing actions bypasses team self-management.
explanation.examTip: Retrospective improvements: add to Sprint Backlog, assign owner, make them small and specific, follow up at next retro. If still failing = meta-retro.

questions.questionText: What does 'respect' as a Scrum value look like in practice?

options.text: Team members agree with each other's decisions to avoid conflict
Team members respect each other's skills, knowledge, and different perspectives, allowing them to collaborate effectively
The Scrum Master must be respected as the team leader
All team members must have equal technical skills to maintain respect

explanation.correct: Respect means Scrum Team members respect each other as capable, experienced individuals with valuable skills and perspectives â€” enabling honest collaboration, healthy conflict, and shared decision-making.
explanation.incorrect: Respect doesn't mean avoiding conflict or agreeing with everything. SM is not 'the leader'. Respect acknowledges different skills, not equal skills.
explanation.examTip: Respect enables courage: you can disagree respectfully. It enables openness: you trust your perspective will be valued. All Scrum values interconnect.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Team is using Scrum for a complex technical project. The Product Owner is new and doesn't understand the technical complexity, often creating Product Backlog items that are too large to complete in a sprint.
questions.questionText: How should the Scrum Master help?

options.text: Take over the Product Owner role temporarily until the PO learns enough about the project
Coach the PO on backlog refinement techniques and facilitate sessions where Developers help the PO understand technical complexity and split stories appropriately
Allow the Developers to ignore the Product Backlog and create their own technical backlog
Ask management to replace the Product Owner with someone more technical

explanation.correct: The SM serves the PO by coaching them on effective backlog management. Involving Developers in refinement helps the PO understand technical constraints and split large items appropriately â€” a core SM accountability.
explanation.incorrect: SM taking over PO role violates accountability separation. Parallel technical backlog undermines PO authority. SM requesting PO replacement oversteps their role.
explanation.examTip: SM coaches PO on: backlog refinement, story splitting, acceptance criteria, working with Developers. Refinement sessions with Developers = practical PO coaching.

questions.questionText: What does 'courage' as a Scrum value require from team members?

options.text: Taking on technically challenging work regardless of risk
Doing the right thing and working on tough problems â€” including raising difficult truths and challenging dysfunctions
Ignoring stakeholder feedback when the team disagrees with it
Working overtime to meet sprint commitments

explanation.correct: Courage in Scrum means the Scrum Team has the courage to do the right thing â€” saying 'no' when capacity is exceeded, raising uncomfortable truths, challenging ineffective processes, and having difficult conversations.
explanation.incorrect: Courage is about doing the right thing, not just technical risk-taking, ignoring stakeholders, or working overtime.
explanation.examTip: Courage in Scrum: saying 'no' to overloading, raising bad news, challenging anti-patterns, questioning the 'way things are done'. Critical for empiricism to work.

questions.scenarioText: A Scrum Master tells the team: 'I'm going to shield you from all external communication and manage all stakeholder relationships myself so you can focus on development.'
questions.questionText: Is this approach consistent with Scrum?

options.text: Yes â€” protecting the team from distractions is a key SM responsibility
No â€” while the SM removes impediments, completely isolating the team from stakeholders prevents the transparency and collaboration that Scrum requires
Yes â€” the SM is the single point of contact for all external communications
No â€” stakeholder management is exclusively the Product Owner's responsibility

explanation.correct: Complete isolation from stakeholders violates Scrum principles. The PO engages stakeholders, Sprint Reviews require stakeholder participation, and the team should have appropriate visibility. The SM protects sprint work, not isolates the team entirely.
explanation.incorrect: SM removing ALL external communication is overprotection â€” it removes transparency and stakeholder feedback, both essential to Scrum.
explanation.examTip: SM protects the team's focus on Sprint Goal (not ad-hoc requests). But stakeholder collaboration (Sprint Review, PO engagement) is essential to Scrum. Protection â‰  isolation.

questions.questionText: What is 'commitment' as a Scrum value?

options.text: Committing to completing all items in the Sprint Backlog
Personally committing to achieving the team's goals and supporting each other
Committing to a fixed project plan at the start of the project
Committing overtime hours to ensure sprint targets are met

explanation.correct: Commitment in Scrum means the Scrum Team commits to the Sprint Goal and to achieving the team's goals â€” it's a commitment to doing their best work together, not a promise to complete a specific list of stories.
explanation.incorrect: Commitment is to the Sprint Goal, not to every Sprint Backlog item. It's not about fixed plans, overtime, or individual promises.
explanation.examTip: Developers commit to the Sprint Goal â€” not to completing every Sprint Backlog item. If new information changes what's possible, the plan adapts while the commitment to the Goal remains.
